clinicalPearls: An acute crystal-induced arthritis caused by calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) crystals, presenting as a hot, swollen, painful joint that clinically mimics gout or septic arthritis
The knee is the most commonly affected joint, followed by the wrist; the first metatarsophalangeal joint, so classic for gout, is less typically involved
Synovial fluid polarised microscopy shows rhomboid or rod-shaped, weakly positively birefringent CPP crystals, in contrast to the needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals of urate
Radiographs frequently show chondrocalcinosis, the linear calcification of fibrocartilage (such as the knee menisci and the triangular fibrocartilage of the wrist) and hyaline cartilage
Attacks may be provoked by intercurrent illness, surgery, or trauma, and increasing age is a strong risk factor
Younger patients or florid, polyarticular disease should prompt a search for metabolic associations, particularly haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia, and hypophosphatasia

Acute attacks are treated with anti-inflammatory measures (a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, colchicine, a corticosteroid, or joint aspiration and injection), as no therapy dissolves CPP crystals
reference.pathophysiology: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals form within cartilage, producing chondrocalcinosis, as a result of altered inorganic pyrophosphate metabolism and calcium handling in ageing or metabolically abnormal cartilage. Shedding of these crystals into the joint space triggers their phagocytosis and an inflammasome-driven inflammatory response similar to that of gout, producing the acute attack. Underlying metabolic disorders such as haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, and hypomagnesaemia predispose to crystal formation, which is why they must be considered, particularly in younger patients.
additionalInvestigations: Joint aspiration with polarised microscopy for positively birefringent rhomboid CPP crystals and to exclude sepsis
Synovial fluid Gram stain, culture, and cell count
Metabolic screen in younger or atypical cases: ferritin and transferrin saturation, calcium and parathyroid hormone, magnesium, and alkaline phosphatase
Ultrasound to detect crystal deposition within cartilage
Serum urate to help distinguish the condition from gout
redFlags: A hot swollen joint that could be septic arthritis until proven otherwise
Chondrocalcinosis in a young patient signalling an underlying metabolic disease
Systemic upset with fever closely mimicking infection
reference.prognosis: Individual acute attacks are self-limiting and respond to anti-inflammatory treatment, but recurrent attacks and chronic CPP-related joint damage are common; because no treatment removes the crystals, management is directed at symptoms and at any underlying metabolic cause.
pitfalls: Assuming a hot joint is gout without confirming the crystal type on microscopy
Missing an underlying metabolic disorder in a young patient with chondrocalcinosis
Expecting urate-lowering therapy to help, when it has no effect on CPP crystals
management: Manage the acute attack with joint aspiration (which also excludes sepsis) and anti-inflammatory treatment using NSAIDs, colchicine or corticosteroids
Intra-articular corticosteroid injection for a single accessible joint once infection has been excluded
Rest, ice and analgesia for the affected joint during an attack
Prophylaxis with colchicine or NSAIDs for frequently recurrent attacks, recognising that no therapy dissolves the crystals
Identify and treat underlying metabolic associations, particularly haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia and hypophosphatasia, especially in younger patients
Manage chronic calcium pyrophosphate arthropathy with physiotherapy and standard osteoarthritis measures
Rheumatology referral for refractory or polyarticular disease
